title: Effects of Cognitive Training in HemOdialysis Patients – The ECHO Study
summary:
Patients with chronic kidney disease — especially those on dialysis — have a significantly increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia. Research shows that up to 80% of dialysis patients are affected, often without being clinically recognized or treated. The causes are multifactorial and not yet fully understood. Possible contributors include reduced cerebral blood flow during dialysis, vascular changes, cardiovascular risk factors, and depression.
Cognitive impairment leads to major losses in quality of life, reduced independence, and difficulties adhering to treatment. It also results in higher healthcare utilization, including more frequent hospital admissions and longer stays.
Currently, no evidence‑based treatment guidelines exist for cognitive impairment in dialysis patients. In other populations, however, cognitive training has been shown to slow cognitive decline and improve daily functioning, with effects lasting up to ten years. Whether these benefits also apply to dialysis patients remains unknown.
Recent studies suggest that dialysis itself may impair cerebral perfusion. Measuring central hemodynamic parameters (e.g., arterial stiffness, pulse wave velocity) may help clarify how vascular function relates to cognitive performance in this population.
The planned study aims to:
systematically assess cognitive impairment in dialysis patients,
identify contributing factors such as vascular stiffness, blood pressure patterns, and psychological factors,
and evaluate whether cognitive training can improve or stabilize cognitive function.
The goal is to generate new insights for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment — ultimately improving patient safety and quality of care for individuals undergoing dialysis.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
·    Patients over the age of 18
·    Patients with end-stage renal failure receiving hemodialysis therapy
·    Informed consent
·    Agreement to undergo further neuropsychological testing during the course of the study, e.g., after 3 months and 1 year
·    German as native language (as the neuropsychological testing and training are language-dependent).
Exclusion criteria:
·    Pre-existing neurological or psychiatric disorders (in particular, history of cerebral infarction, traumatic brain injury, manifest depression, or dementia) that could impair neuropsychological testing.
·    Patients who are under legal guardianship
·    Patients who are unable to understand the patient information or who are unable to cooperate mentally due to their general state of health
·    Insufficient knowledge of the German language
